Progressive shallow-water comfort and rhythmic breathing sequences

reads.note: Best: the outcomes are concrete and the kick/glide numbers are testable; worst: the chapter 3 hook is self-answering, and the 'rolling your cheek' and 'relaxed elbow' wording departs from the brief's high-elbow point.

Best: the outcomes are measurable and match the brief (10 bobs, 15 m kick, 4 side breaths, 25 m). Worst: the 'panics start with goggles' and 'exhausts lungs faster than swimming hard' hooks overstate the brief, and the 300 m goal is a stretch.

chapters.covers: Setting up a watertight goggle seal and establishing comfortable foot placement in chest-deep water.
chapters.hook: Why does leaking water cause instant panic, and how do you fit goggles to prevent it?
chapters.outcome: You can stand and submerge calmly in chest-deep water with clear vision and zero eye irritation.
chapters.title: Goggles and Standing Ground

chapters.covers: Continuous exhalation through your nose and mouth underwater paired with quick inhalation at the surface.
chapters.hook: Holding your breath underwater is the primary reason new swimmers gas out in ten seconds.
chapters.outcome: You can complete ten relaxed bobs in rhythm without holding your breath or feeling breathless.
chapters.title: Blowing Bubbles and Bobbing

chapters.covers: Neutral head alignment looking straight down to raise your hips, and safe recovery to standing.
chapters.hook: Looking forward makes your legs sink instantly, but looking straight down makes you float.
chapters.outcome: You can push off into a five-second streamlined glide and stand up safely by tucking your knees.
chapters.title: The Horizontal Glide

chapters.covers: Straight-leg flutter kicking initiated from the hip flexors with pointed toes and loose ankles.
chapters.hook: Bending your knees turns your legs into underwater brakes rather than engines.
chapters.outcome: You can kick across half the pool with a kickboard while maintaining forward momentum.
chapters.title: Kicking from the Hips

chapters.covers: Fingertip-first entry in line with your shoulder, pulling toward the hip, and high-elbow recovery.
chapters.hook: Swimmers do not pull themselves through water—they anchor their palms and pull water backward.
chapters.outcome: You can pull water efficiently through the full stroke path without straining your shoulders.
chapters.title: The Clean Arm Pull

chapters.covers: Body roll along the spine to take a mouth breath while keeping one goggle lens underwater.
chapters.hook: Lifting your head sinks your hips, but rolling your body brings air directly to you.
chapters.outcome: You can breathe to the side during arm strokes without lifting your head or sinking your hips.
chapters.title: Rotating to Breathe

chapters.covers: Combining slow stroke tempo, rhythmic exhalation, and calm pacing over a full 25-meter distance.
chapters.hook: Swimming slowly is the secret to completing your first continuous lap without gasping for air.
chapters.outcome: You can swim from wall to wall continuously at a sustainable, relaxed pace.
chapters.title: Pacing the Full Length

plan.horizon14: At two weeks, you can swim three consecutive 25-meter lengths with short 30-second rests at each wall.
plan.horizon28: At one month, you can comfortably complete a continuous 200-meter workout using smooth bilateral side breathing.
plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to swim a full 25-meter pool length of freestyle without stopping or touching the bottom.

picture.line: Your buoyant lungs are the hull, your legs act as the steady rudder, and your arms are the rhythmic paddles.
picture.name: A slender kayak

sources.why: Techniques for horizontal balance, hydrodynamics, and low-energy arm propulsion
Standard progression for adult breath control, flotation, and lap readiness

reads.note: Best: the hooks are clear and the chapter order is sound; worst: the last outcomes are vague ('full stroke path', 'relaxed pace'), and 'hip flexors' plus bilateral breathing at day 28 go beyond the brief.

Best: it follows the brief's order and has a clear 25 m end outcome. Worst: the kayak analogy mixes up parts (lungs as hull, legs as rudder), the 'ten seconds' claim is invented, and the 200 m month goal is a stretch.

plans.label: A
plans.note: Best: the chapters follow the brief's outline in order, and the kayak picture covers balance and sinking; worst: the day-7 promise to swim 25 m with side breathing is aggressive, and the chapter 5 outcome has no number.

plans.label: B
plans.note: Best: outcomes are specific and testable (10 bobs, 6 strokes, 5-second glide), and the hooks are punchy; worst: the 500 m in 30 minutes horizon and the claim that breath-holding causes fatigue faster than hard swimming overreach the brief.

plans.label: C
plans.note: Best: the 10-meter build-up pacing idea fits the brief's short segments; worst: the metaphor titles (Exhaust Pipe, See-Saw, Motor) mix several images, and the picture says lungs are buoyancy while the hull is the spine.

plans.label: D
plans.note: Best: the titles follow the brief's outline closely; worst: the log picture is weak, outcomes like 'turn your head into your armpit pocket' are odd and untestable, and the chapter 5 hook is a bare question.

plans.label: E
plans.note: Best: the outcomes are concrete and the kick/glide numbers are testable; worst: the chapter 3 hook is self-answering, and the 'rolling your cheek' and 'relaxed elbow' wording departs from the brief's high-elbow point.

plans.label: F
plans.note: Best: the hooks are clear and the chapter order is sound; worst: the last outcomes are vague ('full stroke path', 'relaxed pace'), and 'hip flexors' plus bilateral breathing at day 28 go beyond the brief.

verdict.why: B and A cover the whole outline in a sound order, with a picture that carries through the chapters, and B's outcomes are the most specific and testable. The lower plans have vaguer outcomes, weaker or muddled pictures, or hooks that give away their answer.

plans.label: A
plans.note: Best: clean three-part structure with accurate sources and a solid causes, collapse, aftermath arc; worst: 'six global powers' and 'most of Europe' overstate the facts, and the Versailles hook is a bit grand.

plans.label: B
plans.note: Best: Versailles chapter ties in the League of Nations and the death toll; worst: chapter 2 mixes the July 1914 declarations with the empires' collapse, and the 'wrong turn' hook is not in the brief.

plans.label: C
plans.note: Best: it separates alliances from the July crisis, which builds well; worst: '20 million soldiers dragged to war in a month' is a made-up claim, and the framing is thin.

plans.label: D
plans.note: Best: the day-by-day July 28 to August 4 outcome is concrete and testable, and the chapters build in order; worst: it credits 'The War That Ended Peace' to MacMillan, which is correct, but the hook says 'mathematically unavoidable' and the empires' collapse and Versailles are crowded into one chapter.

plans.label: E
plans.note: Best: the cleanest progression of causes, then collapse, then aftermath, with the League of Nations and mandates covered; worst: 'six empires' and 'secret treaties' go beyond the brief.

plans.label: F
plans.note: Best: the 'Tripwires' title is compact and ties in the naval arms races; worst: chapter 2 combines the Sarajevo spark with the empires' fall, and 'centuries-old' and 'Europe and Asia' are loose.

verdict.why: E gives the clearest one-theme-per-chapter order (alliances and outbreak, the four empires' fall, then Versailles with the mandates and the League), and its claims stay close to the brief. The lower plans either cram unrelated topics into one chapter or add claims the brief does not support, such as 20 million soldiers.

plans.label: A
plans.note: Best: it follows the brief's order and has a clear 25 m end outcome. Worst: the kayak analogy mixes up parts (lungs as hull, legs as rudder), the 'ten seconds' claim is invented, and the 200 m month goal is a stretch.

plans.label: B
plans.note: Best: the outcomes are measurable and match the brief (10 bobs, 15 m kick, 4 side breaths, 25 m). Worst: the 'panics start with goggles' and 'exhausts lungs faster than swimming hard' hooks overstate the brief, and the 300 m goal is a stretch.

plans.label: C
plans.note: Best: the chapter titles match the brief's outline and the hooks are real open loops. Worst: the floating-log picture is weak and carries little through the chapters, and the 500 m month target is unrealistic.

plans.label: D
plans.note: Best: the picture is the richest, with chapter titles like hull, exhaust pipe, see-saw and motor. Worst: some titles and hooks are cryptic, and the claims that standing stops panic faster than any breathing trick and that swimmers waste half their pull are unsupported.

plans.label: E
plans.note: Best: it has strong, specific hooks such as 'you only need to roll'. Worst: it adds 'pressing your chest down' beyond the brief, and the 500 m in 30 minutes month goal is aggressive.

plans.label: F
plans.note: Best: the facts and chapter order follow the brief closely. Worst: several outcomes have no number or test, and the hooks are long and contain errors, such as 'holding your breath makes you sink'.

verdict.why: B combines measurable, brief-faithful outcomes with an analogy that fits and clear wording. The others either have vague outcomes, weaker pictures, or overreaching claims and month-goal numbers.

plans.label: A
plans.note: Best: ch1 cleanly frames alliances as the foundation and the sources are apt; worst: ch2 puts the Sarajevo spark and the empires' collapse together, and the 'two minor powers' and 'six empires within thirty days' claims are loose.

plans.label: B
plans.note: Best: a clean three-part arc (causes and outbreak, collapse, settlement) with the League of Nations included; worst: 'secret treaties' and 'six-nation war in thirty days' overreach the brief.

plans.label: C
plans.note: Best: dedicates a chapter to the July crisis with vivid hooks; worst: invents the motorcade wrong turn and 'mathematically unavoidable', and 'breakdown' is a grammar slip.

plans.label: D
plans.note: Best: the cleanest build from alliances to outbreak to aftermath with outcomes the reader can check; worst: '20 million soldiers to war in a month' is a made-up number and the framing is generic.

plans.label: E
plans.note: Best: concise and covers all outline parts; worst: chapter 1 jumps straight to the spark, and '20 million deaths' is stated flatly while the brief gives a range of 15 to 22 million.

plans.label: F
plans.note: Best: each chapter has one clear job with testable outcomes like naming the four empires; worst: the hook that the dynasties vanished before fighting ended is slightly off, and chapter 1 crams alliances and Sarajevo together.

verdict.why: The top plans give each chapter a single job in order (alliances, outbreak, aftermath) and set outcomes the reader can test. The lower ones invent details such as the motorcade wrong turn, merge unrelated topics in one chapter, or state numbers the brief does not support.
